justification:
Technical round 2 re-check for /oop-design/factory-builder-singleton/, reading the article fresh from the issue-111 worktree and independently re-fetching both live pages implicated in round 1's two hard-rule findings, plus the Lazy<T> page for the third (low-severity) fix.

Quote 1 (StringBuilder, source [[4]]) is now accurate. Live Remarks text: 'For routines that perform extensive string manipulation (such as apps that modify a string numerous times in a loop), modifying a string repeatedly can exert a significant performance penalty.' The article now reads: '...the documentation warns that "for routines that perform extensive string manipulation," modifying a string repeatedly "can exert a significant performance penalty"[[4]]'. Both quoted fragments are verbatim substrings of the live sentence, in the source's actual order, with only a lowercase 'for' (mid-sentence case adaptation, the same convention already accepted elsewhere in this article and in sibling articles) and the parenthetical aside silently dropped between the two quoted fragments rather than mid-quote. The round-1 defect - singular 'a routine performs' standing in for the source's plural 'routines that perform' - is gone. One very minor, non-blocking style note logged below.

Quote 2 (service-lifetimes, source [[3]]) is now accurate. Live Singleton section text: 'If the app requires singleton behavior, allow the service container to manage the service's lifetime. Don't implement the singleton design pattern and provide code to dispose of the singleton.' The article now reads: '"if the app requires singleton behavior, allow the service container to manage the service's lifetime... don't implement the singleton design pattern and provide code to dispose of the singleton"[[3]]'. The two clauses are verbatim and now appear in the source's actual order (condition, then prohibition), joined by an ellipsis that correctly stands in for the omitted sentence boundary. The round-1 defect - quoting the prohibition before the condition, the reverse of the source's own reasoning - is fully resolved.

Third fix (Lazy<T> concurrency demo, 'lazy-singleton' block) verified as a real, correct improvement. The sample now declares `var instances = new ConcurrentBag<object>();`, adds the actual `AppConfiguration.Instance` object reference from each of 20 parallel tasks, and reports `instances.Distinct(ReferenceEqualityComparer.Instance).Count()` instead of the round-1 version's GetHashCode-based distinctness. `System.Collections.Generic.ReferenceEqualityComparer.Instance` is a real, current BCL API and is a genuine reference-identity comparer, unlike `GetHashCode()`, which the BCL does not document as collision-free. The accompanying prose (paragraph beginning 'Twenty parallel tasks...') correctly explains the change and its rationale ('checked with ReferenceEqualityComparer rather than GetHashCode() - hash codes are not documented to be unique per instance'). This is materially the same fix the round-1 review suggested and it is implemented correctly; the sample still ran and printed 'distinct instances observed: 1' in the verified run-code output.

`node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/oop-design/factory-builder-singleton.md`, run twice consecutively from the issue-111 worktree: PASS both times, blocks=20, executed=10, no flakiness, including the two Parallel.For/ConcurrentBag-based samples and both xUnit samples (one intentionally-failing).

Full fresh read of the rest of the article (not just the three fixed spots) turned up no regressions and no newly introduced errors. Re-verified independently in this round rather than taken on trust from round 1: the Lazy<T> equivalence-table row for `LazyThreadSafetyMode.None` is documented verbatim as 'Not thread safe.' (case-only adapted to 'not thread safe,' in the 'Find the missing guarantee' exercise solution), matching the article's claim exactly and supporting the exercise's reasoning about what `None` gives up. The simple-factory, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, and both Builder sections (HttpRequestBuilder, StringBuilder, WebApplicationBuilder) are unchanged from round 1 and remain correct on this fresh read: template-method structure, matched-family guarantee, fluent chaining via `return this;`, validation inside `Build()`, and the file-based `#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` directive all check out against the code's actual behavior and the cited docs. The two xUnit demonstrations (`bad-singleton-test` failing as designed because both `OrderProcessor` instances share one static `EmailSender.Instance`, then `good-singleton-test` passing after constructor injection) are internally consistent and still constitute the article's central, checkable narrative arc. The GoF chapter-3 classification and citation-by-chapter convention for Gamma et al. are unchanged and remain correct. No new fabricated, altered, or reordered quotations were found anywhere else in the article.

One trivial, non-blocking style note (not a hard-rule violation, not scored down): in the fixed StringBuilder sentence, the comma closing the first quoted fragment ('...string manipulation,"') is placed inside the quotation marks per American convention, even though the live source has no comma at that exact character position (its next character is the parenthetical aside, not a comma) - this is standard practice for repunctuating a quote boundary for grammatical fit and does not alter any word, but a stricter house style could move the comma outside the quotation marks or use ellipsis notation instead.

Not higher than 9.0: no bugs, no unverifiable claims, and no wording-accuracy problems remain, but marking would want to see this same level of scrutiny hold up under an editor's independent read of the whole article rather than only the previously-flagged spots (done here) before treating it as beyond-nits; the one cosmetic quote-boundary-punctuation note keeps this a notch under a flawless 10.

issues.location: 'Builder in the BCL: StringBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder' section, the sentence beginning "`StringBuilder` is the oldest fluent builder in the BCL. Strings are immutable, so..."
issues.problem: The now-corrected quote '"for routines that perform extensive string manipulation,"' places a comma inside the closing quotation mark, but the live source has no comma at that position - the next character in the source is the parenthetical '(such as apps that modify a string numerous times in a loop)', which the article silently omits without an ellipsis. No word is altered and the omission is of an aside outside the load-bearing clause, so this is not a hard-rule violation, but it is a minor departure from strict quote-boundary fidelity.
issues.fixLooksLike: Move the comma outside the closing quotation mark, or insert '[...]' where the parenthetical is omitted, to make the quote boundary exactly match the source's punctuation.
